question: Why have relatively few Indus sites been excavated, how large are the remaining sites, and how much material might future excavation recover?

count_scope.older_summary: A University of Lucknow-hosted chapter cites 2002 sources for at least 1,022 Mature Harappan sites and about 96 excavated. This is an older summary, not a verified current census.
count_scope.newer_observation: Gadekar's 2025 literature review counts 142 excavated Early and Mature Harappan sites, incorporating excavations through 2024.
count_scope.comparison_limit: The time periods differ. This does not measure the precise increase in excavated Mature Harappan sites. Excavated can mean a few trenches; site count does not measure the fraction of surviving deposits excavated.

obstacles.finding: Funding, water, road access and manpower delayed work at Ganweriwala; heat and labour shortages shortened the 2024 season.
The July 2025 report describes a funding interruption, disputed fund release and postponed follow-up work. A subsequent restart was not verified in this search.
Ganweriwala's survey team reported restricted access near the India-Pakistan border and difficult desert conditions.
Lakhanjo-Daro lies beneath expanding modern Sukkur; construction has disturbed and destroyed upper deposits, while some lower deposits survive.
Exposed structures at Mohenjo-daro suffer salt, drainage, groundwater and thermal deterioration, making conservation a continuing obligation.
Excavation entails recording, specialist analysis, storage, conservation and publication. Incomplete publication can prevent researchers from distinguishing absent finds from unreported finds.
obstacles.scope: General archaeological workload supported by the reviewed reports; no comparative national budget or staffing census was conducted.

geographic_inference.finding: Rivers, routes and nearby cities guide hypotheses about settlement function. Proximity alone cannot establish area, date, contemporaneity or political dependence.
geographic_inference.observed_example: Cambridge's Masudpur project reports approximately 6 hectares at Masudpur I and 1 hectare at Masudpur VII in Rakhigarhi's hinterland. Both were investigated by excavation and are comparison cases, not unexcavated examples.
geographic_inference.methods: Surface artifact mapping, mound topography, satellite imagery and geophysics can constrain site boundaries before targeted excavation. Dunes, alluvium, erosion, agriculture and occupation shifts can obscure or alter the apparent footprint.

find_potential.observed_comparison: The pottery section by George F. Dales and Chris Jenkins in the Harappa project report records almost one million sherds from five seasons.
find_potential.count_unit: Pottery fragments; this is not a million intact vessels or inscribed objects.
find_potential.inscription_observation: The same report, printed p. 508, says the first four seasons yielded surprisingly few inscriptions in the excavated areas; 1990 work near a house on Mound E recovered a rich contextual group.
find_potential.judgment: Millions of further ordinary fragments across a sustained civilization-wide program are plausible by analogy with Harappa. This is a qualitative extrapolation, not a calculated forecast. No defensible total for intact artifacts, seals, inscriptions or unique texts was estimated.
needed_for_quantification: Sampled find density by object type and archaeological context
find_potential.priority_inference: A representative mix of villages, workshops, towns and city deposits can improve knowledge of chronology, subsistence, production and writing use. Closely recorded find contexts determine the interpretive value of additional objects.

rights_handling: Only authored summaries, bibliographic pointers and aggregate observations saved. No downloaded papers, images or corpora added.
